title: Pattern Keeper for Cross Stitch: How to Use It and Which PDFs Work

seo.title: Pattern Keeper for Cross Stitch
seo.meta_description: Pattern Keeper for cross stitch: what it does, current Android and stitch-type limits, why PDF compatibility varies and how designers should test files before claiming support.
seo.search_intent: Answer the search intent for pattern keeper for cross stitch: how to use it and which pdfs work with practical, technical and up-to-date guidance.

excerpt: How Pattern Keeper tracks cross stitch PDFs, why some charts import better than others, which limitations still matter and how to test compatibility properly.
content_html:
Pattern Keeper is a chart-reading and progress-tracking app built specifically around cross stitch. When a PDF imports correctly, it can combine chart pages into a continuous working view, recognize symbols, highlight one symbol at a time and let the stitcher mark completed crosses as they work.

Those features are especially useful on large full-coverage charts, where repeatedly scanning multiple printed pages can become tiring. The important caveat is that “PDF” does not automatically mean “fully compatible.” How the chart was generated matters just as much as how it looks in an ordinary reader.

What Pattern Keeper actually does

The app is designed to help follow a chart, not create one. Its main value is turning a supported PDF into a searchable working surface. Instead of manually hunting for one symbol across several pages, the stitcher can highlight that symbol and see the remaining locations more quickly.

Completed stitches can be marked as progress, which makes it easier to return to a large project after a break. A continuous chart view also reduces the mental jump between printed page boundaries.

The original PDF still matters. Materials, finishing instructions, specialty-stitch notes, alternative fabric sizes and other information may not live inside the interpreted chart view.

Current device and stitch-type limitations

As of September 2026, Pattern Keeper's official documentation still lists the app for Android and says an iOS version is not yet available. Anyone considering a device specifically for the app should check the current official requirements before buying because platform support can change.

The official FAQ also states that the interpreted chart currently supports full cross stitches, while backstitch and fractional stitches are not yet supported as recognized stitch types. Those elements still need to be read from the original PDF or another viewer.

That means a chart can be useful in Pattern Keeper without every part of the project being represented there. A pattern with full crosses plus backstitch may still benefit from digital tracking, but the stitcher needs to know where the app's interpretation ends.

Why some PDFs import and others do not

PDF is a container format, not one fixed chart structure. One designer may export selectable text-based symbols and vector grid lines, while another produces flattened images. Both files can look perfect on screen, but Pattern Keeper may interpret them very differently.

Fonts, page construction, unusual legends, multiple separate charts in one document and extra grid-like images can all affect import. The official support information explicitly notes that PDF complexity makes universal compatibility impossible to guarantee.

For the stitcher, the safest approach is to import the actual purchased file before committing to a huge project and verify symbol recognition, page alignment and the thread key.

How to verify an imported chart before stitching

Choose a distinctive area in the original PDF and compare it with the imported version. Check the number of rows, the position of a recognizable feature and several symbols around it. This catches alignment errors before hundreds of crosses are marked against the wrong interpretation.

Test symbol search on a common color and on one that appears only a few times. Confirm that the thread reference shown in the app matches the PDF legend. If the chart spans many pages, inspect at least one former page boundary.

Keep a clean copy of the original PDF. Progress data should be treated as a separate working layer so the purchased master remains available if the app, device or annotations change.

What designers need to test before claiming compatibility

Pattern Keeper publishes guidance for designers and current WinStitch/MacStitch releases include a dedicated export option for Pattern Keeper-compatible PDFs. That is helpful, but using the export option is not the same as validating the finished product.

The exported file should be opened on a realistic Android device, imported from start to finish and compared with the master chart. Symbol recognition, legend mapping, coordinates, page joins and basic performance should all be checked.

Large files also need practical testing. A technically compatible chart can still be frustrating if zooming, highlighting or navigation becomes sluggish because the PDF is unnecessarily heavy.

How a premium MAKE PDF should handle compatibility

If we advertise Pattern Keeper compatibility, that claim should apply to the exact downloadable file and should be based on a real import test. A product page can state that full-cross tracking was verified while reminding customers that backstitch or fractional stitches must still be followed in the source PDF when present.

The PDF itself should remain excellent without Pattern Keeper: clear ten-stitch grid lines, distinct symbols, stable coordinates, readable pagination, full materials, dimensions, strand counts and specialty instructions. Digital compatibility is an additional feature, not a substitute for a complete document.

Because app behavior can evolve, compatibility notes should be dated or versioned internally so we know which export was tested. That creates a stronger premium promise: the customer receives a file designed to print well, read well in a standard viewer and, where stated, work predictably in Pattern Keeper too.
